To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) The use of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) in breast cancer has increased in the last 10 years, and is currently recommended in the management of early breast cancer in selected patients; (ii) The main goal of NACT is to achieve a pathological complete response (pCR); (iii) The pCR rate is higher in HER2-positive and triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) patients; (iv) The pCR is associated with a better prognosis;

the current international standards of NAST protocols are not fully applied in the daily practice of Spanish breast pathologists, and that a consensus is needed to standardize the definition of pathological complete response (PCR).
breast pathologists should have a central role in the management of NAST, and the definition of pCR is a crucial step in the process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of pathologists and their contribution in the management of neoadjuvant therapy.
the following questions: What are the international guidelines on NAST?
the following questions: What is the role of the pathologist in the NAST?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the current international recommendations on the role of the pathologist in the management of NAST are not followed in Spain, with the exception of the use of immunohistochemistry to assess residual disease in the breast.

the use of NAST has been increasing in Spain in recent years and that the majority of Spanish pathologists use a combination of histological and immunohistochemical (IHC) methods to define pathological complete response in their daily practice.
the current recommendations for the use of NAST for patients with breast cancer are based on clinical trials and are not yet fully established in clinical practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a need for a consensus among pathologists and oncologists to establish a standardized approach for reporting NAST protocols in Spain.
there is a need to standardize the definition of pathological response, and that the Spanish pathologists are aware of the need for a more precise definition.

the Spanish breast pathologists have reached an agreement on the following points: the use of NAST is increasing in Spain and is a valid alternative to surgery; there is a need for a multidisciplinary team in order to establish the most appropriate treatment; and that the use of NAC should be based on the type of breast cancer, the patient's age and the patient's wishes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of breast pathologists has evolved from a descriptive to a predictive role, with an active part to play in the management of patients undergoing NAST.
breast pathologists are essential in the management of NAST protocols and that the current international standards should be adapted to our clinical reality.

breast surgeons and pathologists must work in tandem in order to ensure that patients receive optimal care and that they are able to make the right decisions about the treatment that is best for them.
